match.reason: The new point covers both how a text's historical and social context shapes its ideas and how readers respond, but the closest bank points each teach only one half: eng-context-reception covers reader context and eng-context-composition covers how the writer's context shapes the text, so neither matches the brief closely enough to reuse or adapt.

draft.title: Context and a text
card: Context is the world a text comes from or is read in. It includes the time and place it was written, and the social and cultural values of that time.
the events and conditions of the period. A novel written during a war may be shaped by fear, loss or hope for peace.
the beliefs about what is normal or right in a society, such as ideas about class, gender or duty. A writer may accept these values or challenge them.
Readers bring their own context too. A reader today may respond to a text differently from a reader when it was first published.
draft.remember: Context shapes what a text says and how readers respond to it.

a.q: Why does a student studying a novel look at the context in which it was written?
opts: It helps explain the ideas the text explores
It replaces the need to read the text closely
It shows what the author ate and wore each day
It proves the text has only one correct reading
a.why: Knowing the time, place and values behind a text helps explain why its ideas take the shape they do. It adds to close reading and does not replace it, and it does not prove there is only one reading.
a.clue: Context helps you understand why the text's ideas look the way they do.

b.q: A novel was published in 1920 and shows a young woman who is expected to give up her job when she marries. A student reads it today and is surprised by this. What does this show?
opts: The text reflects its era, and today's reader has other values
The writer was wrong about how people lived in that era
Readers in 1920 and today would respond in the same way
The novel's ideas are unrelated to the time it was written
b.why: The expectation about marriage and work reflects the values of the writer's society. The student's surprise comes from the values of today's reader, so both contexts matter. It is not a mistake, and responses can differ across time.
b.clue: Think about two contexts: the one the text came from and the one the reader is in.

a.q: A student writes that a novel's focus on hunger and lost jobs makes sense, as it was written during an economic depression. What is the student doing?
opts: Using historical context to explain the text's ideas
Using today's reader's context to explain a response
Showing that the writer challenges the values of the era
Showing that the text can have only one correct reading
a.why: The depression is an event and condition of the period, so it is historical context, and the student uses it to explain the novel's ideas. The comment is about when the text was written, not about how a reader today responds, and it says nothing about the writer challenging values.
a.clue: Is the student talking about the writer's time or the reader's time?
